about.f1: 14 languages, each with a full translation of the interface
about.f2: 25 live features, all fetched from free public data sources
about.f3: No account, no cookie, no advertising, no cost
about.p1: I built this site because most weather pages bury a number you need under three you do not. Every one of the 25 features here is explained in plain language on the guide page, and where a value is estimated or borrowed from somewhere else, the card says so instead of pretending otherwise.
about.p2: It is one person's work: no framework, no build step, no tracking, no API keys, and no paid translation service. The code is deliberately plain so that it can be read, checked and corrected.
about.p3: If something here is wrong, the honest fix is to change it — so corrections are genuinely welcome.

guide.h1: Every number on this site, explained in plain English
guide.honest.b1p: CO₂ is measured near cities, not at your window. It carries a “not local weather” label rather than being dressed up as a local reading.
guide.honest.b1t: 🌍 Global values get a global badge
guide.honest.b2p: Ground temperature comes from a model grid, not a thermometer in your street. The card says “estimated” and explains which estimate it is.
guide.honest.b3p: Near the coast you get wave height and sea temperature. Inland, the card is removed entirely instead of showing a blank box that looks broken.
guide.honest.b4p: At high latitudes the sun does not always rise. The page says “no sunset — midnight sun” or “polar night” instead of printing 12:00 AM.
guide.honest.b4t: 🌙 Polar day and night are named
guide.honest.b5p: The sunshine figure is a forecast for the entire day, so it does not drop to zero at noon. The label says so.
guide.honest.b6p: Water leaving the soil is quoted in millimetres per hour. Multiplying it by 24 to get a daily figure would be wrong, so we do not.
guide.honest.b6t: 💧 Evaporation is a rate, not a total
guide.honest.b7p: When a value is unavailable the card shows a dash and a reason. We never substitute a plausible-looking number to keep the layout tidy.
guide.honest.b8p: Live, estimated, conditional, global, or background — each of the 25 features is labelled above, so you can tell at a glance how much weight to give it.
guide.honest.intro: Most of the trust problems on weather sites come from showing a confident number that was never measured. These are the specific cases, and what happens instead.
guide.honest.title: What we will not fake
guide.how.intro: Nothing here is typed in by hand, and nothing is generated by an AI. Every value on the forecast page is fetched from a public weather API when you open the page, and the page says how old it is.
guide.how.outro: The forecast models behind the numbers are the national ones — ECMWF, GFS, ICON and others — blended by Open-Meteo. This site does not run its own model and does not claim to.
guide.how.s1p: Search by city name or use your location. The name is turned into coordinates once, and those coordinates are what every request uses.
guide.how.s2p: A small proxy fetches from Open-Meteo and caches the reply for ten minutes. Caching is what keeps the site inside the free tier — one visitor does not mean one upstream call.
guide.how.s3p: Each card reads its own field. If a field is missing, the card says so instead of showing a zero. There is no invented fallback anywhere on the page.
guide.how.title: Where these numbers actually come from
guide.intro: Weather sites throw words at you — “surface pressure”, “CAPE”, “aerosol optical depth” — and never say what they mean. This page does. Each feature gets a plain label, a short note on what it tells you, and an honest badge for how much to trust it. The first 25 come from the original feature notes and keep their exact wording. Two more were added afterwards and sit in their own group at the end, so the original list stays intact. Read it once, then head to the forecast.
guide.note.p: The first 25 notes cover the features a weather site can honestly show. The other 30 variables on the official climate list need satellites or yearly reports, so nothing truthful could be displayed for them — they are left out rather than faked.
guide.q.intro: The short answers. Each one is about something a reader has genuinely questioned while using a weather site.
guide.q.title: Questions people actually ask
guide.q1p1: The weather data is free but rate-limited. A single scraper in a loop can use up the day's allowance and break the site for everyone else. The check is a one-time speed bump, it takes about a second, and it happens once per visit rather than once per page.
guide.q1p2: Be aware of what it is: a deterrent, not a lock. It stops casual scraping and bulk copying. It would not stop someone determined, because everything it does happens in your browser where it can be read. Real protection needs a server-side check such as Cloudflare Turnstile, and this project deliberately stays free and key-less instead.
guide.q1p3: There is no account, no email, no cookie and no tracking pixel. Everything the check needs stays in your browser.
guide.q1s: Why does the site ask me to prove I am not a bot?
guide.q2p1: The accuracy is the underlying model's, not this site's. This page displays what Open-Meteo returns without adjusting it. In general, a three-day forecast is far more reliable than a seven-day one, and rainfall intensity is the least reliable field of all — the models agree on “rain likely” long before they agree on how much.
guide.q2p2: A useful rule: trust the shape of the next 24 hours, treat anything past day five as a trend rather than a plan.
guide.q2s: How accurate is a forecast here?
guide.q3p1: Different models, different grids, different update times. Your phone may be showing a reading from a station near you while this page shows an interpolated value for the grid cell containing your city — which can be several kilometres across.
guide.q3p2: Urban heat is the other factor. A grid cell that averages a city with its surrounding countryside will read cooler than a thermometer on a hot street.
guide.q3s: Why is the temperature different from my phone's weather app?
guide.q4p1: CAPE measures how much energy a rising parcel of air has available — high values mean the atmosphere is primed for thunderstorms. The raw unit (joules per kilogram) is not intuitive, so the storm card converts it to a 0–100 score and labels the result.
guide.q4p2: It is an indicator, not a warning service. For official thunderstorm warnings, follow your national meteorological agency.
guide.q4s: What is CAPE, and why is the storm score a percentage?
guide.q5p1: No. Every value is fetched live, so with no connection there is nothing to show and the page tells you so with a retry button. It is a website, not an installed app, and it does not claim to work offline.
guide.q5s: Does this work offline, or as an app?
guide.q6p1: No. The weather, air-quality, marine and geocoding data all come from Open-Meteo's free tier, and the map outlines come from OpenStreetMap volunteers. There is no API key in this project and no billing account behind it.
guide.q6p2: The trade-off is the free tier's limits: it is intended for non-commercial use, with a rough ceiling of about ten thousand requests a day. If this ever became popular enough to exceed that, the honest options are to pay, to cache harder, or to slow down — not to quietly start scraping someone else.
guide.q7p1: Because the other thirty on the official climate list need satellites or yearly reports rather than a live forecast. Showing them would mean showing something that is not actually being measured, so they are deliberately left out — and the note at the bottom of this page names that decision rather than hiding it.
